newsitem.title: USA: Corn, soybeans and orange juice lead commodities up.
newsitem.headline: Corn, soybeans and orange juice lead commodities up.

text.p: Soybean prices rose Monday as traders worried about hot weather hurting the young Brazilian crop, while corn prices posted gains due to strong exports.

Cattle and hog prices rose, and orange juice soared on worries about freeze damage in Florida. Overall, the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures ended 2.54 points higher at 243.65.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, the heat and dryness in South America outweighed a slowdown in U.S. soybean exports. March soybeans ended 2-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $7.49-3/4.
Weekend rains missed key growing areas in Rio Grande do Sul, a key producer state in Brazil, the No. 2 soybean exporter after the United States.
"They didn't get all that much rain in Brazil but there is some in the forecast," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.

Traders bet that a lack of moisture might continue and pose a threat to Brazilian yields. This helped them ignore a weekly report from the Agriculture Department that said only 16.7 million bushels of soybeans were inspected for export at U.S. ports last week, against 35.3 million a week earlier.
March corn ended 2-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $2.75, aided by strong figures from the government export report.
A total of 38.9 million bushels of corn were inspected in the week ended Jan. 23 following 42.4 million a week earlier, with both numbers seen pointing to strong demand.
That export interest also helped corn traders shrug off selling during the day in response to Friday's surprisingly low Agriculture Department report for cattle at feedlots.

The report put the number of cattle placed in December in the top seven feeding states at 98 percent of last year's level, well under the average trade guess of 108.2 percent. Fewer cattle on feed means less feed demand for corn.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, February live cattle ended 0.325 cent a pound higher at 64.975 cents, and March feeder cattle ended 0.725 cent a pound higher at 69.250.
"The market closed about the way the report led you to believe," said Don Roose, President U.S. Commodities Inc.
Hog prices also rose as winter storms in the Midwest cut farmer marketings of hogs. February lean hog futures closed 0.225 cent a pound higher at 77.175 cents.

At the New York Cotton Exchange, jitters continued about the extent of damage to Florida citrus after temperatures plunged on Jan. 18-19. March frozen concentrate orange juice futures ended up 10 cents a pound at 93.50 cents.

The Florida Agricultural Statistics Service said Monday an estimated 180,000 boxes of navel oranges were harvested in the week ended Jan. 26, down from 266,000 boxes a week earlier and 222,000 boxes in the week ended Jan. 12.
An estimated 7,308,000 boxes of early and mid oranges were harvested in the week ended Jan. 26, down from 11,053,000 boxes a week earlier and 9,352,000 boxes two weeks ago.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, February heating oil rose 0.52 cent a gallon to 67.29 cents on forecasts of below normal temperatures and an expected decline in refined product output.
"It looks like we are going to have freezing weather this week which has given the market impetus to trade back up," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products for Paribas Futures Inc.

"There is a good case for refined products. Production is expected to decline with the refinery turnarounds, but crude continues to weigh down the market due to weak cash prices," said," said Kevelson.
March crude oil closed down 11 cents a barrel at $23.94, and February gasoline down 0.13 cent a gallonr at 67.62 cents.
